questions.q: What should the first step in building a safety eval suite look like, according to this lesson?
options: Writing the phrase "the model should be safe" as the test criterion
Naming the specific behavior of concern in concrete, testable terms
Collecting as many test cases as possible before deciding what they test
Skipping directly to automated scoring without defining a target behavior
questions.explain: A vague goal like "be safe" isn't testable; a concrete, specific behavior of concern is what makes writing a real test case possible.

questions.q: Why does this lesson argue that diversity among test cases matters more than sheer volume?
options: Because more test cases always take longer to run than fewer ones
Because models can learn to pattern-match one specific phrasing style without the underlying behavior actually generalizing to different phrasings of the same risk
Because volume has no cost in compute or review time
Because diverse test cases are always easier to automate than similar ones
questions.explain: Twenty genuinely different approaches to the same risk surface failure modes that two hundred near-duplicates of one template would never reveal.

questions.q: What is a key limitation of a model-as-judge scoring setup that this lesson warns about?
options: It cannot be used on more than ten test cases at a time
It scales cheaply but inherits its own blind spots, so it should be paired with human review of a genuine random sample
It is always more expensive than full human review
It eliminates the need for any held-out or rotated test data
questions.explain: An automated judge can share or create blind spots, which is why human spot-checking a real random sample — not just borderline-flagged cases — matters.

questions.q: Why does this lesson recommend tracking eval results across successive model versions rather than treating a single run as sufficient?
options: Because a single eval run is a snapshot, and the real value is in the trend — whether a concerning behavior improves, stays flat, or shifts into a disguised form
Because running the eval more than once is required by most government regulations
Because model versions never change behavior in any measurable way
Because a single run always produces an unreliable random score
questions.explain: Longitudinal tracking reveals whether an unrelated update caused a concerning behavior to genuinely improve or merely move to a less obvious form.

questions.q: Why should a meaningful portion of a safety eval suite be kept unpublished and periodically rotated?
options: To make the suite harder for the lab's own engineers to use
To resist contamination, where eval items leaking into training data would inflate future scores through memorization rather than genuine safety improvement
Because published eval items are legally required to be deleted after one year
Because rotation has no connection to the eval's reliability
questions.explain: This directly echoes the contamination pitfall covered earlier in the chapter — held-out, rotated data is the main practical defense against it.
